title: "Elastic Constants: E, ν, λ, μ"

## Poisson's ratio — what does it mean?

Pull a bar and it usually gets thinner — that lateral response is set by $\nu$. Try the
presets below: cork ($\nu\approx0$), typical metals ($\nu\approx0.3$), rubber
($\nu\approx0.499$, nearly incompressible), and auxetic foam ($\nu<0$, gets *fatter*
when stretched).

```{=html}
<iframe class="interactive-frame" src="../interactives/poisson_intuition.html"></iframe>
```

## Lamé constants ↔ (E, ν)

$$
\mu = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{E\nu}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}, \qquad K = \frac{E}{3(1-2\nu)}
$$

```{=html}
<iframe class="interactive-frame" src="../interactives/lame_constants.html"></iframe>
```

## What do λ and μ mean physically?

$\mu$ resists pure shape change (shear). $\lambda$ is subtler — it's the stress that
appears sideways *only when lateral strain is prevented* (confined loading), not something
you'd feel in a free pull test.

